subtopic_detail: COVID-19 severity assessment and dexamethasone indication
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with 5 days of cough, fever, and progressive dyspnoea. He has type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3b. A SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test is positive. He is commenced on supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs at 4 L/min to maintain saturation above 92%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 136/78 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 89% on room air (94% on 4 L NP), T 38.4 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.2 x10^9/L, CRP 124 mg/L, lymphocytes 0.6 x10^9/L, Cr 186 micromol/L (baseline 152), chest X-ray bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention at this stage?

options.text: Oral nirmatrelvir-ritonavir 300/100 mg twice daily for 5 days to reduce viral replication
options.rationale: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is indicated for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in patients at high risk of progression, ideally within 5 days of symptom onset and BEFORE the need for supplemental oxygen. Once a patient requires oxygen, the disease has progressed beyond the antiviral-responsive phase into the hyperinflammatory phase. (Source: Australian National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce)

options.text: IV remdesivir 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg daily as the sole additional treatment
options.rationale: Remdesivir may have a role in hospitalised patients with COVID-19, but the single most impactful intervention in patients requiring supplemental oxygen is systemic corticosteroids. Remdesivir alone without dexamethasone would omit the treatment with the strongest mortality benefit in this severity tier. (Source: National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce; RECOVERY trial)

options.text: Commence empiric IV co-amoxiclav for presumed bacterial co-infection based on the CRP
options.rationale: Bacterial co-infection in acute COVID-19 is uncommon in the first week of illness. Empiric antibiotics are not recommended unless there is a clear clinical indication such as purulent sputum, lobar consolidation, or procalcitonin elevation suggesting superinfection. CRP alone is insufficient. (Source: National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce; eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral paracetamol and supportive care only until further oxygen escalation is required
options.rationale: Withholding corticosteroids in a patient already requiring supplemental oxygen would miss the proven mortality benefit demonstrated in the RECOVERY trial. Dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality in patients requiring oxygen or ventilation. Waiting for further deterioration is not appropriate. (Source: National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days alongside standard supportive care
options.rationale: The RECOVERY trial demonstrated that dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduced 28-day mortality by approximately one-third in patients requiring supplemental oxygen. This patient requires oxygen and is therefore in the appropriate severity tier for corticosteroid therapy. Dexamethasone is the cornerstone of treatment for hospitalised COVID-19 patients with hypoxia. (Source: National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce; RECOVERY trial)

explanation.summary: COVID-19 management is stratified by severity. Antiviral agents such as nirmatrelvir-ritonavir are most effective in the early viral replication phase before oxygen requirement. Once a patient requires supplemental oxygen, the disease has entered the hyperinflammatory phase where systemic corticosteroids provide the greatest benefit. The RECOVERY trial established that dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduces 28-day mortality by about one-third in oxygen-dependent patients. Dexamethasone does not benefit and may harm patients who do not require oxygen.
key_points: Dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days is the cornerstone treatment for hypoxic COVID-19
Antivirals are for early mild-to-moderate disease before oxygen requirement
Corticosteroids do not benefit patients who are not hypoxic
Bacterial co-infection is uncommon in early COVID-19 and antibiotics should not be empiric
RECOVERY trial showed one-third mortality reduction in oxygen-requiring patients
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone in COVID-19 follows a severity threshold - it reduces mortality in patients requiring oxygen (number needed to treat approximately 8 for ventilated patients) but shows a non-significant trend toward harm in patients not requiring respiratory support.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, stable ischaemic heart disease, and COPD presents to his GP on day 2 of mild COVID-19 symptoms confirmed by rapid antigen test. He has a persistent dry cough and mild fatigue but no dyspnoea or hypoxia. His regular medications include rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler, and salbutamol as needed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm irregular, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air, T 37.8 C
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to antiviral therapy?

options.text: Switch rivaroxaban to enoxaparin, switch ticagrelor to clopidogrel, and suspend atorvastatin during the course
options.rationale: This addresses all major ritonavir-CYP3A4 interactions: enoxaparin replaces rivaroxaban (avoiding DOAC level increase), clopidogrel replaces ticagrelor (clopidogrel is not a CYP3A4 substrate for its active metabolite), and atorvastatin is suspended for the treatment plus washout period (avoiding rhabdomyolysis risk from statin accumulation). This allows nirmatrelvir-ritonavir to be used safely. (Source: AMH; National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce)

options.text: Withhold rivaroxaban and ticagrelor during the 5-day nirmatrelvir-ritonavir course plus 3 days after
options.rationale: Withholding both anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy in a patient with AF and ischaemic heart disease creates unacceptable thromboembolic risk. The correct approach is to either manage interactions with dose adjustments and bridging or choose an alternative antiviral. Complete cessation of both agents is not appropriate. (Source: AMH; eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Prescribe molnupiravir as an alternative antiviral that avoids these drug interactions entirely
options.rationale: Molnupiravir does not inhibit CYP3A4 and avoids ritonavir interactions, but it has lower efficacy than nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and is generally reserved as a second-line option. The preferred approach is to attempt interaction management with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir first, or use remdesivir if interactions cannot be managed. (Source: National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce; AMH)

options.text: Withhold ticagrelor and switch rivaroxaban to enoxaparin for the treatment course plus washout period
options.rationale: While switching rivaroxaban to therapeutic enoxaparin avoids the DOAC interaction, withholding ticagrelor in a patient with ischaemic heart disease increases acute coronary risk. Additionally, atorvastatin levels will still rise markedly. A comprehensive interaction management plan addressing all affected medications is needed rather than partial adjustment. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Commence nirmatrelvir-ritonavir at standard dose with no medication adjustments needed
options.rationale: Ritonavir is a potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor. Co-administration with rivaroxaban and ticagrelor, both CYP3A4 substrates, significantly increases their plasma levels, raising the risk of major bleeding. Atorvastatin levels also increase substantially. Interaction management is mandatory before commencing. (Source: AMH; National COVID-19 Clinical Evidence Taskforce)

explanation.summary: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is the most effective oral antiviral for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in high-risk patients when started within 5 days of symptoms. However, the ritonavir component is a potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor that creates significant drug interactions with many common medications. Rivaroxaban, ticagrelor, and atorvastatin are all CYP3A4 substrates whose levels increase substantially with ritonavir. Managing these interactions requires temporary medication switches for the treatment course plus a 3-day washout. When interaction management is not feasible, alternative antivirals should be considered.
key_points: Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein causing major drug interactions
Rivaroxaban and ticagrelor levels increase significantly with ritonavir co-administration
Switching to enoxaparin and clopidogrel avoids the interaction while maintaining therapy
Atorvastatin must be suspended due to rhabdomyolysis risk from CYP3A4 inhibition
Interaction management should cover the 5-day course plus 3-day ritonavir washout
explanation.pearls: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated primarily by CYP2C19, not CYP3A4, so unlike ticagrelor and prasugrel it can be co-administered with ritonavir without loss of antiplatelet effect or dangerous level increases.

subtopic_detail: Levodopa wearing-off phenomenon recognition and management
stem: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson disease diagnosed 6 years ago presents with increasing difficulty with mobility over the past 4 months. He was initially well controlled on levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily. He now describes predictable worsening of tremor, rigidity, and slowness in the 30 to 60 minutes before each dose is due. He is independent with activities of daily living during on-periods.

data_table.Examination: Currently in off-state: moderate resting tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity bilateral upper limbs, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial adjustment to manage this complication?

options.text: Add entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose to prolong peripheral levodopa availability
options.rationale: Entacapone is a COMT inhibitor that prolongs levodopa half-life and is a valid option for wearing-off. However, the recommended first step for predictable wearing-off is to increase dosing frequency (shorter intervals) before adding adjunct agents, as this is simpler and addresses the pharmacokinetic issue directly. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Increase dosing frequency to four times daily with a reduced individual dose to maintain total daily levodopa
options.rationale: Predictable end-of-dose wearing-off is best managed initially by shortening the dosing interval while adjusting individual doses to avoid peak-dose dyskinesia. Moving from TDS to QID with the same total daily dose provides more consistent dopaminergic stimulation. This is recommended as the first-line adjustment before adding adjunct therapies. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Switch entirely to a sustained-release levodopa formulation at the same total daily dose
options.rationale: Sustained-release levodopa has less predictable absorption and lower bioavailability than standard formulations. It is sometimes used as an adjunct at night but is not recommended as a complete replacement for standard levodopa for daytime wearing-off due to erratic absorption. (Source: eTG: Neurology; AMH)

options.text: Add pramipexole as a dopamine agonist to provide more continuous dopaminergic stimulation
options.rationale: Adding a dopamine agonist is a valid strategy for motor fluctuations but carries significant risks including impulse control disorders, excessive daytime somnolence, and hallucinations, particularly in older patients. Simpler dose interval adjustments should be tried first. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Refer for deep brain stimulation assessment given the failure of current oral medication
options.rationale: Deep brain stimulation is reserved for patients with disabling motor fluctuations or dyskinesia despite optimised medical therapy. This patient has not yet had any dose adjustment and is still functionally independent during on-periods. Medical optimisation must be exhausted before surgical referral. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

explanation.summary: Wearing-off is the most common motor complication in Parkinson disease on chronic levodopa therapy, typically appearing after 5 to 10 years of treatment as nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons progressively decline, reducing buffering capacity. The initial management is to shorten the dosing interval while keeping total daily levodopa constant. If this is insufficient, COMT inhibitors (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (rasagiline), or dopamine agonists can be added as adjunct therapy. Deep brain stimulation is reserved for medically refractory motor fluctuations.
key_points: Wearing-off presents as predictable return of motor symptoms before the next levodopa dose
First-line management is to shorten the dosing interval while maintaining total daily dose
COMT inhibitors and MAO-B inhibitors are second-line adjuncts for wearing-off
Dopamine agonists carry risks of impulse control disorders especially in older patients
Deep brain stimulation is a last resort after optimal medical therapy
explanation.pearls: Wearing-off typically develops after 5 to 10 years of levodopa therapy and correlates with progressive loss of presynaptic dopaminergic neuron storage capacity - the remaining neurons cannot buffer levodopa levels between doses, leading to pulsatile stimulation of postsynaptic receptors.

subtopic_detail: Impulse control disorder on dopamine agonist in Parkinson disease
stem: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson disease diagnosed 3 years ago returns for routine review. His motor symptoms are well controlled on pramipexole 1 mg three times daily. His wife reports he has spent over $18,000 on online gambling in the past 2 months and has also developed compulsive online shopping. He has no prior psychiatric history and had no behavioural issues before starting pramipexole.

data_table.Medications: Pramipexole 1 mg TDS, no other medications
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral resting tremor, minimal rigidity, normal gait

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this complication?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy while continuing pramipexole at the current dose
options.rationale: CBT may have a supportive role, but the primary management is to reduce or cease the causative dopamine agonist. Continuing pramipexole at the same dose while attempting behavioural therapy alone will not resolve a pharmacologically driven impulse control disorder. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Add an SSRI for impulse control and maintain pramipexole at the current effective dose
options.rationale: SSRIs are not effective treatment for dopamine agonist-induced impulse control disorders. The mechanism is excessive mesolimbic dopaminergic stimulation, and the definitive management is dose reduction or cessation of the dopamine agonist. (Source: eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Gradually taper pramipexole and substitute levodopa to maintain motor symptom control
options.rationale: Dopamine agonist-induced impulse control disorders require gradual dose reduction or cessation of the agonist. Motor symptoms should be managed by substituting levodopa. Abrupt cessation risks dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (apathy, anxiety, pain). Impulse control disorders affect approximately 15 to 20% of patients on dopamine agonists and are a class effect. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Reduce pramipexole to the lowest effective motor dose and monitor gambling behaviour monthly
options.rationale: Dose reduction alone may be insufficient if the impulse control disorder is severe and causing significant financial harm. Complete cessation is often required. Monitoring alone without active management of a harmful behavioural complication is inadequate given the severity of financial loss. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Parkinson's Disease 2017)

options.text: Switch pramipexole to ropinirole as an alternative dopamine agonist with lower impulse risk
options.rationale: Impulse control disorders are a class effect of all dopamine agonists, not unique to pramipexole. Switching to ropinirole would not resolve the problem as both drugs act on D2/D3 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway. The appropriate management is to taper the entire class. (Source: eTG: Neurology; AMH)

explanation.summary: Impulse control disorders are a recognised class effect of dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease, mediated by stimulation of D3 receptors in the ventral striatum and mesolimbic reward pathway. They include pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality, and binge eating. The prevalence is approximately 15 to 20% on dopamine agonists. Management requires gradual agonist cessation with levodopa substitution. Patients should be warned about this risk before starting any dopamine agonist, and regular screening during treatment is recommended.
key_points: Impulse control disorders are a class effect of all dopamine agonists via D3 receptor stimulation
Prevalence is approximately 15 to 20% on dopamine agonist therapy
Management is gradual cessation of the agonist with levodopa substitution
Abrupt withdrawal risks dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome
All patients should be screened for ICD before and during dopamine agonist therapy
explanation.pearls: Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (DAWS) occurs in approximately 15% of patients upon agonist cessation and presents with anxiety, panic, dysphoria, insomnia, and pain that does not respond to levodopa - gradual tapering over weeks to months is essential.

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome from acute dopaminergic withdrawal
stem: A 74-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease on levodopa-carbidopa 250/25 mg four times daily and entacapone 200 mg with each dose is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. The admitting team holds her Parkinson medications due to vomiting and being nil by mouth. On day 3 she develops high fevers, severe generalised rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, diaphoresis, and tachycardia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, BP 168/98 mmHg fluctuating, RR 26/min, T 40.2 C
data_table.Investigations: CK 8,400 U/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, Cr 198 micromol/L (baseline 82), lactate 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of this deterioration and the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Septic shock from pneumonia - escalate antibiotics and commence IV vasopressors
options.rationale: While ongoing pneumonia could contribute, the combination of severe rigidity, hyperthermia, and massively elevated CK following dopaminergic medication withdrawal is characteristic of Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome, not simple sepsis. Sepsis alone would not explain the CK of 8,400 U/L or the severe rigidity. Antibiotics should continue but the dopaminergic crisis must be addressed. (Source: eTG: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Parkinson Disease)

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from antibiotic interaction - cease all serotonergic agents and give cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome presents with clonus, hyperreflexia, and agitation rather than the lead-pipe rigidity and obtundation seen here. The temporal relationship with dopaminergic medication withdrawal and the presence of severe rigidity with markedly elevated CK points to Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome. (Source: eTG: Neurology; AMH)

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by anaesthetic exposure during intubation procedures
options.rationale: There is no mention of anaesthetic exposure or surgical procedures. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetic agents or succinylcholine, not by dopaminergic medication withdrawal. The clinical timeline clearly implicates medication cessation. (Source: ANZCA)

options.text: Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome - urgently reinstate dopaminergic medications via nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome (also called neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome) occurs when dopaminergic medications are abruptly withdrawn. It presents identically to NMS with hyperthermia, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability, and rhabdomyolysis. Treatment is urgent reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy, which can be given via nasogastric tube if the patient cannot take oral medications. IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis and ICU monitoring are also required. (Source: eTG: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Parkinson Disease)

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from newly commenced antiemetic - cease metoclopramide and give dantrolene
options.rationale: While dopamine-blocking antiemetics can precipitate NMS in Parkinson patients, there is no mention of metoclopramide or any neuroleptic being given. The clinical picture is fully explained by abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal. Even if an antiemetic contributed, the immediate priority would be reinstating dopaminergic therapy rather than dantrolene alone. (Source: eTG: Neurology; AMH)

explanation.summary: Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome is a life-threatening emergency caused by abrupt withdrawal or rapid dose reduction of dopaminergic medications. It is clinically identical to neuroleptic malignant syndrome - presenting with hyperthermia, severe rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability, and rhabdomyolysis. It can occur when medications are held during intercurrent illness, particularly when patients are nil by mouth. Treatment is urgent reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation for rhabdomyolysis, and ICU-level monitoring. Mortality approaches 4% even with treatment.
key_points: Parkinson medications should never be abruptly stopped during intercurrent illness
Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome mimics NMS with rigidity, hyperthermia, CK elevation, and AKI
Nasogastric or dispersible levodopa should be used if the patient cannot swallow
Dopamine-blocking antiemetics such as metoclopramide are contraindicated in Parkinson disease
Domperidone is the preferred antiemetic as it does not cross the blood-brain barrier
explanation.pearls: Dispersible levodopa-benserazide (Madopar Dispersible) can be given via nasogastric tube in nil-by-mouth Parkinson patients - it should be pre-dissolved in water and administered within 30 minutes as it degrades rapidly in solution.

subtopic_detail: Vascular dementia vs Alzheimer disease discrimination
stem: A 76-year-old man is brought by his daughter for assessment of progressive cognitive decline over 12 months. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and a previous lacunar stroke 2 years ago. His daughter reports his memory decline occurred in distinct steps rather than gradually, with a noticeable worsening after each episode of transient confusion. He has prominent executive dysfunction and psychomotor slowing but relatively preserved episodic memory in the early stages.

data_table.Investigations: MMSE 22/30, MoCA 18/30 (significant executive impairment), MRI brain shows multiple lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter with moderate small vessel disease
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD, metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Alzheimer disease with concurrent cerebrovascular disease and mixed pathology
options.rationale: Mixed dementia is possible but the stepwise decline pattern, executive-predominant profile with relatively preserved episodic memory, extensive vascular risk factors, and MRI showing multiple lacunar infarcts and white matter disease all point more strongly to vascular dementia as the primary diagnosis. Alzheimer typically presents with insidious progressive episodic memory loss. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Dementia 2018)

options.text: Lewy body dementia with vascular comorbidity and parkinsonism overlap
options.rationale: Lewy body dementia is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism. There is no mention of hallucinations or parkinsonian features, and the stepwise rather than fluctuating pattern is more consistent with vascular dementia. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Dementia 2018)

options.text: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presenting with cognitive decline and gait disturbance
options.rationale: The classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus is dementia, gait apraxia, and urinary incontinence. While there may be some gait changes from small vessel disease, the MRI shows lacunar infarcts and white matter disease rather than ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement. The stepwise pattern also favours vascular dementia. (Source: eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Frontotemporal dementia with executive dysfunction as the predominant cognitive domain
options.rationale: Frontotemporal dementia typically presents before age 65 with prominent behavioural changes (apathy or disinhibition) and language difficulties rather than stepwise decline in the context of cerebrovascular disease. The extensive vascular risk factors, multiple infarcts on MRI, and stepwise course strongly favour a vascular aetiology. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Dementia 2018)

options.text: Vascular dementia secondary to cerebral small vessel disease and strategic infarcts
options.rationale: The combination of stepwise cognitive decline, executive-predominant cognitive impairment with relatively preserved episodic memory, extensive vascular risk factors, history of lacunar stroke, and MRI evidence of multiple lacunar infarcts and small vessel disease is consistent with vascular dementia. The temporal relationship between cognitive steps and possible vascular events further supports this diagnosis. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Dementia 2018)

explanation.summary: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia in Australia and is characterised by cognitive decline temporally related to cerebrovascular disease. Key clinical features that distinguish it from Alzheimer disease include stepwise rather than gradual decline, early executive dysfunction with relatively preserved episodic memory, psychomotor slowing, and prominent vascular risk factors. MRI typically shows multiple infarcts, lacunae, and white matter hyperintensities. Management focuses on secondary stroke prevention (anticoagulation for AF, antihypertensives, statins) rather than cholinesterase inhibitors, which have limited evidence in pure vascular dementia.
key_points: Stepwise decline is characteristic of vascular dementia vs insidious decline in Alzheimer disease
Executive dysfunction and psychomotor slowing predominate over episodic memory loss early on
MRI showing multiple lacunar infarcts and white matter disease supports the diagnosis
Secondary stroke prevention is the cornerstone of management
Cholinesterase inhibitors have limited evidence in pure vascular dementia but may help mixed pathology
explanation.pearls: The Hachinski Ischaemic Score was developed to differentiate vascular from degenerative dementia - a score of 7 or above suggests vascular aetiology, while 4 or below suggests Alzheimer disease.

subtopic_detail: Cholinesterase inhibitor initiation criteria and monitoring in Alzheimer disease
stem: A 78-year-old woman is diagnosed with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease after comprehensive assessment including neuropsychological testing and MRI. Her MMSE is 20/30. She lives with her husband and manages most activities of daily living with some prompting. Her medical history includes stable angina, hypertension, and a permanent pacemaker inserted 4 years ago. Her resting HR is 62 bpm. Her current medications are aspirin 100 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily.

data_table.Investigations: ECG: ventricular paced rhythm, rate 62 bpm, no conduction abnormality on native beats
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention for her cognitive decline?

options.text: Commence donepezil 5 mg daily and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Donepezil is first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease under the PBS. Initiation dose is 5 mg daily, titrated to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks. The pacemaker mitigates the cholinergic risk of bradycardia, making this patient a suitable candidate. Baseline ECG and pulse rate monitoring are still recommended. Treatment is continued while MMSE remains above 10. (Source: AMH; PBS Cholinesterase Inhibitor Authority)

options.text: Commence memantine 5 mg daily as first-line given the cardiac history and bradycardia risk
options.rationale: Memantine is PBS-listed for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease (MMSE 10 to 14) as monotherapy, not mild-to-moderate. While it avoids cholinergic cardiac effects, using it off-label when the patient has a pacemaker that mitigates bradycardia risk is not appropriate. Donepezil remains first-line for this severity. (Source: AMH; PBS)

options.text: Commence rivastigmine transdermal patch to avoid gastrointestinal side effects of oral agents
options.rationale: Rivastigmine is an alternative cholinesterase inhibitor, but it is not PBS-listed as a first-line agent for Alzheimer disease in Australia. Donepezil and galantamine are the first-line PBS-subsidised options. Rivastigmine patches are primarily indicated for Parkinson disease dementia. (Source: AMH; PBS)

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy and commence a structured cognitive stimulation program as sole treatment
options.rationale: Cognitive stimulation therapy is a valuable non-pharmacological adjunct, but evidence supports cholinesterase inhibitors as the first-line pharmacological treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease. Deferring medication when a patient meets PBS criteria and has no absolute contraindications denies a proven symptomatic benefit. (Source: eTG: Neurology; NICE Dementia 2018)

options.text: Commence combined donepezil 10 mg and memantine 10 mg from the outset for maximal benefit
options.rationale: Combination therapy is not recommended at initiation. Australian guidelines recommend starting with a cholinesterase inhibitor at the lower dose and titrating. Memantine can be added later for moderate-to-severe disease or if cholinesterase inhibitors alone are insufficient. Starting both simultaneously increases adverse effect risk without proven incremental benefit at the mild-to-moderate stage. (Source: AMH; PBS)

explanation.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease in Australia. Donepezil is the most commonly prescribed, starting at 5 mg daily and titrating to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks. PBS authority requires an MMSE of 10 or above and a confirmed diagnosis. Key adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms and bradycardia; a pre-existing pacemaker mitigates the bradycardia risk. Memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease. Regular MMSE monitoring determines continuation.
key_points: Donepezil 5 mg daily is first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease under PBS
Titrate to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated
PBS continuation requires MMSE above 10 at reassessment
Cholinesterase inhibitors carry a risk of bradycardia that requires ECG monitoring
Memantine is PBS-listed for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease only
explanation.pearls: PBS authority for donepezil requires an MMSE of 10 or above confirmed by a specialist, with reassessment at 6 months - cessation is recommended if MMSE drops below 10 as benefit is unlikely to continue.

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive dementia workup - CJD vs paraneoplastic vs autoimmune
stem: A 62-year-old previously well woman is referred urgently by her GP with a 6-week history of rapidly progressive cognitive decline, personality change, and myoclonic jerks. She was functioning normally 2 months ago. Over the past 2 weeks she has developed visual hallucinations, gait ataxia, and is now unable to care for herself. There is no relevant family history. MRI brain shows bilateral cortical and caudate DWI restriction. CSF protein is mildly elevated at 0.52 g/L with no cells.

data_table.Investigations: MRI: bilateral cortical ribboning and caudate head DWI restriction, EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 to 2 Hz, CSF: protein 0.52 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, WCC 0, RCC 0

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Autoimmune encephalitis - send CSF and serum anti-NMDAR and anti-LGI1 antibodies
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis can present with rapid cognitive decline but typically affects younger patients and usually shows CSF pleocytosis. The absence of CSF cells, the prominent myoclonus, the cortical ribboning pattern on DWI, and periodic sharp waves on EEG are highly specific for prion disease rather than autoimmune encephalitis. (Source: eTG: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: CJD)

options.text: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease - send CSF RT-QuIC assay and 14-3-3 protein
options.rationale: The combination of rapidly progressive dementia over weeks, myoclonus, ataxia, cortical ribboning with caudate DWI restriction on MRI, and periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG is classic for sporadic CJD. CSF RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) has over 90% sensitivity and near 100% specificity and has largely replaced 14-3-3 protein as the definitive antemortem diagnostic test. (Source: eTG: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: CJD)

options.text: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis - send anti-Hu and anti-CV2 antibodies and CT body
options.rationale: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis can cause subacute cognitive decline and seizures, but it typically affects the medial temporal lobes rather than showing cortical ribboning and caudate DWI restriction. Myoclonus and periodic sharp waves on EEG are far more characteristic of CJD. Paraneoplastic workup may be reasonable as a differential but is not the primary diagnosis here. (Source: eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Hashimoto encephalopathy - send anti-TPO antibodies and commence a steroid trial
options.rationale: Hashimoto encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis) can present with cognitive decline and myoclonus, but the MRI pattern of cortical ribboning with caudate restriction and periodic sharp waves on EEG are not typical. It should be considered as a treatable mimic, but the clinical and investigative pattern here is classic for CJD. (Source: eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Whipple disease of the CNS - send CSF Tropheryma whipplei PCR and duodenal biopsy
options.rationale: CNS Whipple disease is a rare cause of progressive cognitive decline with myoclonus, but it typically has a much longer prodrome with systemic features (arthralgia, diarrhoea, weight loss) and does not produce the cortical ribboning DWI pattern or periodic sharp waves characteristic of CJD. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: CJD)

explanation.summary: Sporadic CJD is the most common human prion disease and presents with rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months accompanied by myoclonus, ataxia, visual disturbance, and pyramidal or extrapyramidal signs. The diagnostic triad is DWI restriction in cortex and/or basal ganglia on MRI, periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG, and positive CSF RT-QuIC assay. RT-QuIC has largely replaced 14-3-3 protein testing due to superior specificity. The median survival is approximately 5 months. There is no disease-modifying treatment; management is supportive and palliative.
key_points: CJD presents with rapidly progressive dementia over weeks with myoclonus and ataxia
MRI shows cortical ribboning and caudate/putamen DWI restriction
EEG periodic sharp wave complexes are seen in approximately 60% of sporadic CJD
CSF RT-QuIC assay has greater than 90% sensitivity and near 100% specificity
Median survival is approximately 5 months with no disease-modifying treatment
explanation.pearls: CSF RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) detects misfolded prion protein by amplifying its ability to convert normal recombinant PrP into amyloid fibrils in vitro - it has largely replaced 14-3-3 protein testing because 14-3-3 is elevated in many causes of rapid neuronal destruction and lacks specificity.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a sudden-onset severe headache reaching maximal intensity within 60 seconds while showering. She describes it as the worst headache of her life. She has no neurological deficits on examination. A non-contrast CT brain performed within 2 hours of onset is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 142/88 mmHg, RR 16/min, T 36.9 C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, fundoscopy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure that the normal CT excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage and discharge with follow-up
options.rationale: CT brain sensitivity for SAH declines from approximately 98% at 6 hours to 93% at 12 hours and further with time. A normal CT within 6 hours reduces but does not eliminate SAH risk. Lumbar puncture or CT angiography is required to complete the evaluation. Australian practice supports LP as the gold standard second-line investigation. (Source: Stroke Foundation; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Perform MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging to exclude ischaemic stroke as the cause
options.rationale: This presentation with a thunderclap headache and no focal deficit does not suggest ischaemic stroke as the primary concern. The immediate priority is excluding SAH with lumbar puncture. MRI may have a role later if LP is negative and an alternative diagnosis such as RCVS is considered. (Source: eTG: Neurology; Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia and elevated red blood cell count
options.rationale: After a normal CT in the setting of thunderclap headache, lumbar puncture is the standard next investigation to detect small-volume SAH missed on CT. Xanthochromia (detected by spectrophotometry) is the key finding and develops 12 hours after haemorrhage, peaking at approximately 1 week. If LP is also negative, further investigation for RCVS and other causes should follow. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange CT angiography of the cerebral vessels to directly assess for aneurysm or vasospasm
options.rationale: CTA is increasingly used and some centres accept CTA combined with CT as sufficient to exclude SAH within 6 hours. However, the traditional Australian approach and Stroke Foundation guidelines still recommend LP as the next step after normal CT, particularly when the CT was performed early and sensitivity for small bleeds is not 100%. CTA may follow if SAH is confirmed or if RCVS is suspected. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines 2022)

options.text: Administer IV sumatriptan as a diagnostic and therapeutic trial for severe migraine headache
options.rationale: Triptans are contraindicated in unexcluded SAH and RCVS. Sumatriptan is a vasoconstrictor and could worsen vasospasm. A thunderclap headache must be assumed to be SAH until proven otherwise, and the investigation pathway must be completed before any migraine-specific treatment is considered. (Source: eTG: Neurology; AMH)

explanation.summary: Thunderclap headache - defined as severe headache reaching maximal intensity within 60 seconds - is a red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. The standard investigation pathway is non-contrast CT brain (sensitivity approximately 98% within 6 hours) followed by lumbar puncture if CT is negative. LP should ideally be performed at least 12 hours after onset to allow xanthochromia to develop. If both CT and LP are negative for SAH, the differential includes reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and pituitary apoplexy.
key_points: Thunderclap headache must be investigated for SAH regardless of the presence of neck stiffness
CT sensitivity for SAH declines over time from approximately 98% at 6 hours
Lumbar puncture is the standard next step after a normal CT in thunderclap headache
Xanthochromia by spectrophotometry is the key LP finding for SAH
RCVS is the most common diagnosis when both CT and LP are negative for SAH
explanation.pearls: Xanthochromia should be assessed by spectrophotometry rather than visual inspection - visual detection requires bilirubin concentration above 3 micromol/L, while spectrophotometry detects levels as low as 0.5 micromol/L, significantly reducing false negatives.

subtopic_detail: RCVS recognition and management after SAH exclusion
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with her third thunderclap headache in 10 days, each triggered by Valsalva manoeuvre or sexual activity. She uses sumatriptan for migraine and takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. Non-contrast CT and lumbar puncture after the first episode were normal. CT angiography now shows segmental narrowing of bilateral middle cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries in a string-of-beads pattern.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 148/92 mmHg, RR 14/min, T 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: no haemorrhage or infarct, CTA: multifocal segmental vasoconstriction bilateral MCA and PCA territories, LP (day 1): no xanthochromia, opening pressure 16 cmH2O

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oral nimodipine and monitor for delayed cerebral infarction over the coming weeks
options.rationale: Nimodipine is sometimes used empirically in RCVS based on its role in aneurysmal SAH vasospasm, but the evidence is limited and it is not universally recommended as initial management. The critical first step is to identify and cease vasoactive triggers. Nimodipine may be considered adjunctively. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: RCVS; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Perform urgent conventional cerebral angiography to plan endovascular vasodilator therapy
options.rationale: Conventional angiography is the gold standard for demonstrating vasoconstriction but carries procedural risk. Endovascular intervention with intra-arterial vasodilators is reserved for RCVS complicated by progressive neurological deficit or infarction, not for uncomplicated recurrent thunderclap headache. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: RCVS)

options.text: Commence high-dose IV methylprednisolone for presumed primary CNS vasculitis
options.rationale: Primary CNS vasculitis can mimic RCVS on angiography but typically presents with gradual onset, CSF pleocytosis, and progressive rather than thunderclap headaches. The normal CSF, recurrent thunderclap pattern with Valsalva triggers, and known vasoactive medication use all favour RCVS over vasculitis. Corticosteroids may worsen RCVS outcomes. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: RCVS; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Cease sumatriptan and the combined oral contraceptive and prescribe supportive analgesia only
options.rationale: RCVS is a clinical-radiological syndrome of recurrent thunderclap headaches with reversible segmental cerebral vasoconstriction. The most important initial step is identifying and ceasing vasoactive triggers. Triptans and combined hormonal contraceptives are both recognised precipitants. RCVS is typically self-limiting over 1 to 3 months with vasoconstriction resolving spontaneously. Supportive analgesia, rest, and avoidance of Valsalva triggers form the core management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: RCVS; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin to prevent stroke from the vasoconstriction
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is not indicated in RCVS and may increase the risk of haemorrhagic complications, as RCVS can be associated with convexal subarachnoid haemorrhage and intracerebral haemorrhage. The vasoconstriction is reversible and management focuses on trigger removal and supportive care. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: RCVS)

explanation.summary: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is characterised by recurrent thunderclap headaches over 1 to 3 weeks with segmental vasoconstriction of cerebral arteries that resolves within 3 months. Triggers include triptans, SSRIs, sympathomimetics, cannabis, and combined hormonal contraceptives. The key diagnostic features are normal CSF (distinguishing it from vasculitis) and multifocal vasoconstriction on CTA or MRA. Management centres on cessation of vasoactive triggers and supportive care. Complications include ischaemic stroke and cortical SAH in a minority of cases.
key_points: RCVS presents with recurrent thunderclap headaches over days to weeks
CSF is normal in RCVS, which differentiates it from primary CNS vasculitis
CTA or MRA shows multifocal segmental vasoconstriction in a string-of-beads pattern
Triptans, SSRIs, combined OCP, and sympathomimetics are recognised triggers
Vasoconstriction resolves spontaneously within 1 to 3 months after trigger removal
explanation.pearls: Corticosteroids are associated with worse outcomes in RCVS, possibly by impairing the natural resolution of vasoconstriction - this contrasts with primary CNS vasculitis where corticosteroids are the mainstay, making the distinction between these two entities critical before treatment.

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation and component ratios
stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He has an obvious open femoral fracture and a rigid distended abdomen. Despite 2 litres of IV crystalloid his blood pressure remains 72/40 mmHg. The trauma team activates the massive transfusion protocol. O-negative packed red blood cells are being administered.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg (after 2 L crystalloid), RR 30/min, SpO2 94% on 15 L non-rebreather, T 35.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L, platelets 112 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, pH 7.18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood product ratio to guide ongoing resuscitation?

options.text: Packed red blood cells alone until haemoglobin exceeds 100 g/L then reassess coagulation
options.rationale: Red cells alone will not address the dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy that develops in massive haemorrhage. Balanced resuscitation with plasma and platelets is essential to prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. RBC-only strategies are associated with worse outcomes. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZSBT)

options.text: Packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma in a ratio of 4:1 with platelets only if count drops below 50
options.rationale: A 4:1 RBC-to-FFP ratio provides inadequate early coagulation factor replacement. Current evidence supports near-equal ratios of red cells to plasma to maintain haemostatic function. Waiting for platelet count to fall below 50 before supplementation delays critical haemostatic support. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; PROPPR trial)

options.text: Packed red cells and cryoprecipitate only, withholding FFP due to the risk of transfusion reactions
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate provides fibrinogen and factor VIII but does not replace the full spectrum of coagulation factors found in FFP. Both products are needed in massive haemorrhage. Transfusion reaction risk does not justify withholding life-saving haemostatic products in this context. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZSBT)

options.text: IV tranexamic acid 1 g and crystalloid only until crossmatched blood is available for transfusion
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an important adjunct in trauma haemorrhage (CRASH-2 trial showed mortality benefit when given within 3 hours) but it does not replace blood product resuscitation. Waiting for crossmatched blood when O-negative is available and the patient is in haemorrhagic shock would be harmful. (Source: CRASH-2 trial; NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)

options.text: Packed red cells, FFP, and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio with cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen falls below 1.5 g/L
options.rationale: Current Australian and international massive transfusion protocols recommend a balanced 1:1:1 ratio of packed red cells to FFP to platelets, approximating whole blood composition. This approach reduces mortality from coagulopathy. Cryoprecipitate is added when fibrinogen falls below 1.5 g/L (this patient's fibrinogen of 1.1 g/L already meets this threshold). Tranexamic acid should also be given within 3 hours of injury. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZSBT; PROPPR trial)

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion is defined as replacement of one or more total blood volumes within 24 hours, or transfusion of more than 10 units of packed red cells. Australian protocols recommend a balanced 1:1:1 ratio of red cells to FFP to platelets to prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Cryoprecipitate is indicated when fibrinogen falls below 1.5 g/L. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be administered within 3 hours of injury based on the CRASH-2 trial. Point-of-care testing with viscoelastic haemostatic assays can guide targeted component therapy.
key_points: Massive transfusion protocol uses a 1:1:1 ratio of red cells to FFP to platelets
Cryoprecipitate is indicated when fibrinogen falls below 1.5 g/L
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of injury reduces mortality in trauma haemorrhage
The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy must be actively prevented
Point-of-care viscoelastic testing can guide targeted blood product replacement
explanation.pearls: In the PROPPR trial, 1:1:1 transfusion ratio achieved haemostasis faster than 1:1:2 and reduced death from exsanguination at 24 hours - the 30-day mortality difference narrowly missed significance, but the haemostatic benefit is now standard of care.

subtopic_detail: Citrate toxicity and hypocalcaemia during massive transfusion
stem: A 28-year-old woman is undergoing massive transfusion for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with estimated blood loss exceeding 4 litres. She has now received 10 units of packed red cells, 10 units of FFP, and 2 pooled doses of platelets over 90 minutes. The surgical team reports ongoing haemorrhage. She develops perioral paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm in her free hand, and the ECG monitor shows a prolonged QTc of 520 ms with new ST depression.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 24/min, T 34.8 C
data_table.Investigations: Ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L (reference 1.12 to 1.32), K 5.9 mmol/L, pH 7.22, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 1.8

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of the QTc prolongation and the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Citrate toxicity causing hypocalcaemia - administer 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride IV over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Citrate anticoagulant in stored blood products chelates ionised calcium. During massive transfusion, the liver's capacity to metabolise citrate is overwhelmed, causing symptomatic hypocalcaemia. The ionised calcium of 0.78 mmol/L confirms the diagnosis. IV calcium chloride (10 mL of 10% = 6.8 mmol Ca) is preferred over calcium gluconate in critical settings as it delivers three times more elemental calcium per ampoule. Ongoing calcium replacement is required with each transfusion cycle. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZSBT)

options.text: Hyperkalaemia from stored red cell potassium leakage - administer IV calcium gluconate and insulin-dextrose
options.rationale: While hyperkalaemia from stored blood is a real risk (potassium leaks from stored RBCs over time), the primary ECG finding here is QTc prolongation, which is characteristic of hypocalcaemia, not hyperkalaemia. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, shortened QT, and widened QRS. The ionised calcium of 0.78 mmol/L confirms hypocalcaemia as the dominant electrolyte problem requiring urgent correction. (Source: ANZSBT; NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)

options.text: Hypothermia-induced cardiac instability - commence active external rewarming before any electrolyte correction
options.rationale: While hypothermia at 34.8 C can prolong the QTc and impair coagulation, the degree of hypothermia here is mild and would not explain the severity of QTc prolongation to 520 ms with carpopedal spasm. The ionised calcium level confirms citrate toxicity as the primary issue. Rewarming is important but does not address the hypocalcaemia. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)

options.text: Dilutional coagulopathy causing myocardial ischaemia - administer cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma
options.rationale: Dilutional coagulopathy is present (fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 1.8) and cryoprecipitate is needed, but coagulopathy does not cause QTc prolongation or carpopedal spasm. The ECG changes and neuromuscular symptoms are explained by the critically low ionised calcium of 0.78 mmol/L requiring urgent calcium replacement as the immediate priority. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZSBT)

options.text: Transfusion-related acute lung injury causing hypoxic cardiac strain - cease transfusion and give IV furosemide
options.rationale: TRALI presents with acute respiratory distress, bilateral infiltrates, and hypoxia within 6 hours of transfusion. This patient's symptoms are neuromuscular (paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm) and cardiac (QTc prolongation), not respiratory. Ceasing transfusion in active haemorrhage would be life-threatening. The findings are explained by citrate-induced hypocalcaemia. (Source: ANZSBT)

explanation.summary: Citrate toxicity is an under-recognised complication of massive transfusion. All stored blood products contain citrate anticoagulant, which chelates ionised calcium. When transfusion rates exceed the liver's capacity to metabolise citrate - typically above 1 unit every 5 minutes - symptomatic hypocalcaemia develops. Clinical features include perioral paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm, QTc prolongation, hypotension, and in severe cases cardiac arrest. Ionised calcium should be monitored every 30 minutes during massive transfusion. IV calcium chloride is preferred over calcium gluconate in critical haemorrhage.
key_points: Citrate in stored blood products chelates ionised calcium during massive transfusion
QTc prolongation, paraesthesia, and carpopedal spasm are classic hypocalcaemia signs
Ionised calcium should be monitored every 30 minutes during massive transfusion
10 mL of 10% calcium chloride provides 6.8 mmol elemental calcium per ampoule
Calcium gluconate provides only 2.2 mmol per ampoule and requires three times more volume
explanation.pearls: IV calcium chloride delivers 6.8 mmol of elemental calcium per 10 mL ampoule versus 2.2 mmol for calcium gluconate - this threefold difference matters in massive transfusion where rapid correction is needed, though calcium chloride must be given via a central line or large-bore peripheral to avoid tissue necrosis.

subtopic_detail: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis - exchange transfusion indications
stem: A 24-year-old man with known HbSS sickle cell disease presents with severe bilateral lower limb and back pain consistent with a vaso-occlusive crisis. He is being managed with IV morphine patient-controlled analgesia, IV fluids, and supplemental oxygen. On day 2 of admission he develops acute right-sided hemiplegia with expressive aphasia. His baseline Hb is typically 80 to 90 g/L and his current Hb is 72 g/L with HbS fraction 78%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 148/88 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, T 38.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 72 g/L, HbS 78%, reticulocytes 280 x10^9/L, LDH 620 U/L, bilirubin 68 micromol/L, CT brain: no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention for this complication?

options.text: Commence IV alteplase at standard stroke dose given the CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: IV thrombolysis is not the standard of care for sickle cell-associated stroke. The mechanism is primarily vaso-occlusive and haemolytic rather than thromboembolic. Exchange transfusion to reduce HbS fraction is the definitive treatment. Thrombolysis carries a high bleeding risk in SCD patients who may have underlying vasculopathy. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

options.text: Arrange urgent automated red cell exchange transfusion targeting HbS fraction below 30%
options.rationale: Acute ischaemic stroke in sickle cell disease is an indication for urgent exchange transfusion (manual or automated apheresis) to reduce HbS fraction below 30% while maintaining Hb below 100 g/L to avoid hyperviscosity. Exchange transfusion is superior to simple transfusion as it reduces HbS rapidly without increasing total Hb. Stroke is the most serious vascular complication of SCD and recurrence risk without chronic transfusion is approximately 70%. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

options.text: Perform simple top-up transfusion to raise Hb to 100 g/L and reassess neurological status
options.rationale: Simple transfusion raises total Hb but does not adequately reduce the HbS fraction. In acute stroke, rapid HbS reduction is essential. Additionally, raising Hb above 100 g/L in SCD risks hyperviscosity and further vaso-occlusion. Exchange transfusion achieves HbS reduction without raising total Hb. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with IV heparin for presumed large vessel occlusion
options.rationale: SCD-associated stroke has a different pathophysiology from cardioembolic or atherothrombotic stroke. The primary mechanism involves sickling-mediated endothelial damage and large vessel vasculopathy. Exchange transfusion to reduce HbS is the treatment of choice, not anticoagulation. Anticoagulation may be considered adjunctively in some cases but is not first-line. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines)

options.text: Administer IV dexamethasone to reduce cerebral oedema and refer for urgent thrombectomy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are associated with rebound vaso-occlusive events in SCD and are generally avoided. Thrombectomy is not established for SCD-associated stroke, which involves a different vasculopathy from standard large vessel occlusion. The priority is exchange transfusion. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

explanation.summary: Stroke occurs in approximately 11% of HbSS patients by age 20 and is one of the most devastating complications of sickle cell disease. The mechanism involves sickling-mediated endothelial injury, large vessel vasculopathy, and intimal hyperplasia rather than conventional atherothrombosis. Emergency exchange transfusion to reduce HbS below 30% is the standard of care. After an initial stroke, chronic transfusion therapy to maintain HbS below 30% is required to prevent recurrence, which otherwise approaches 70% within 3 years.
key_points: Acute stroke in SCD requires urgent exchange transfusion targeting HbS below 30%
Simple transfusion is inadequate as it does not sufficiently reduce HbS fraction
Total Hb should not exceed 100 g/L post-transfusion to avoid hyperviscosity
IV thrombolysis is not standard of care for SCD-associated stroke
Chronic transfusion therapy is required after initial stroke to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: Transcranial Doppler velocities above 200 cm/s in the internal carotid or middle cerebral artery identify children with SCD at high stroke risk - the STOP trial showed chronic transfusion reduces first stroke incidence by 92% in this population.

subtopic_detail: Acute splenic sequestration crisis in adult HbSC disease
stem: A 22-year-old woman with known HbSC disease presents with sudden-onset left upper quadrant pain, nausea, and light-headedness. She has had no prior splenic complications. Her baseline Hb is typically 110 g/L. On examination she appears pale and diaphoretic. Her spleen is palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin, which is new from her last clinic visit 3 months ago where the spleen was not palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, BP 82/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 92% on room air, T 37.6 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 52 g/L (baseline 110), reticulocytes 420 x10^9/L, platelets 68 x10^9/L (baseline 220), LDH 890 U/L, bilirubin 82 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Splenic infarction with haemolytic crisis - commence IV fluids and simple red cell transfusion
options.rationale: Splenic infarction causes pain but does not typically cause the acute rapid splenic enlargement, profound anaemia with Hb drop of 58 g/L, and thrombocytopaenia seen here. The rapidly enlarging spleen with acute anaemia is characteristic of splenic sequestration, not simple infarction. Simple transfusion must be given cautiously in sequestration to avoid hyperviscosity when red cells are released from the spleen. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

options.text: Hypersplenism from chronic congestion - arrange elective splenectomy within the coming weeks
options.rationale: Hypersplenism develops gradually with chronic splenomegaly and mild cytopaenias. This presentation is acute with rapid-onset splenomegaly, profound anaemia, and haemodynamic instability consistent with acute sequestration. Elective management is inappropriate when the patient is in hypovolaemic shock. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines)

options.text: Acute splenic sequestration - commence cautious transfusion targeting Hb 80 to 90 g/L and plan splenectomy
options.rationale: Acute splenic sequestration occurs when sickled red cells trap rapidly in the spleen, causing acute splenomegaly, profound anaemia (Hb drop of greater than 20 g/L below baseline), thrombocytopaenia, and hypovolaemic shock. It is more common in HbSC disease adults because the spleen may not have auto-infarcted as in HbSS. Cautious transfusion is critical - target Hb 80 to 90 g/L only, as auto-transfusion from the spleen when sequestration resolves can cause dangerous Hb overshoot and hyperviscosity. Splenectomy is recommended after a single sequestration episode in adults. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

options.text: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 - check parvovirus serology and transfuse to baseline Hb
options.rationale: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 causes profound anaemia with inappropriately low reticulocytes due to erythroid precursor destruction. This patient has markedly elevated reticulocytes at 420 x10^9/L, indicating active marrow response, which excludes aplastic crisis. The acute splenomegaly and thrombocytopaenia point to sequestration. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines)

options.text: Haemolytic crisis with DIC - commence exchange transfusion and IV heparin for coagulopathy
options.rationale: While haemolysis markers are elevated, the thrombocytopaenia here reflects platelet trapping in the congested spleen, not DIC. DIC would show prolonged PT/APTT and elevated D-dimer with fibrinogen consumption. The acute splenomegaly with Hb drop and thrombocytopaenia is pathognomonic for splenic sequestration. Heparin in acute SCD crisis would increase bleeding risk. (Source: BSH Sickle Cell Guidelines; HSANZ)

explanation.summary: Acute splenic sequestration is a life-threatening emergency in sickle cell disease where sickled red cells rapidly pool in the spleen, causing acute splenomegaly, profound anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, and hypovolaemic shock. While it most commonly affects young children with HbSS, adults with HbSC disease or HbS-beta-thalassaemia are at risk because their spleens often remain functional. A key management principle is cautious transfusion to Hb 80 to 90 g/L only, because when the sequestration episode resolves, trapped cells are released back into circulation, causing dangerous Hb overshoot. Splenectomy is recommended after a single episode in adults.
key_points: Acute splenic sequestration presents with rapid splenomegaly, profound anaemia, and thrombocytopaenia
HbSC patients retain splenic function into adulthood unlike HbSS patients
Transfusion must be cautious to avoid Hb overshoot when sequestered cells are released
Target Hb of 80 to 90 g/L only during the acute episode
Splenectomy is recommended after a single episode in adults to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: HbSC patients retain splenic function into adulthood because HbC polymerises less aggressively than HbS, resulting in less splenic infarction - this paradoxically makes them susceptible to acute splenic sequestration at ages where HbSS patients are already functionally asplenic.

subtopic_detail: ABG interpretation - mixed acid-base disorder identification
stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and COPD presents with 3 days of vomiting, polyuria, and increasing confusion. He has been unable to take his metformin or fluids for 3 days. He appears dehydrated with Kussmaul breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 32/min deep, SpO2 94% on room air, T 37.2 C
data_table.Investigations: ABG: pH 7.18, pCO2 22 mmHg, pO2 92 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L, BE -18. Na 138 mmol/L, K 5.8 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, BSL 38.2 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, Cr 248 micromol/L, urea 22 mmol/L

lead_in: Which acid-base disturbance is present?

options.text: Simple high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation only
options.rationale: Anion gap is 138 - (98 + 8) = 32, confirming a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from DKA. Winter formula predicts expected pCO2 = 1.5 x 8 + 8 = 20 mmHg. The actual pCO2 of 22 mmHg is close but slightly higher. The delta-delta ratio (change in AG / change in HCO3) = (32-12) / (24-8) = 20/16 = 1.25, which is between 1 and 2, suggesting a pure HAGMA. However, the elevated urea and creatinine suggest a component of pre-renal AKI contributing additional unmeasured anions. (Source: eTG: Respiratory; BMJ Best Practice: DKA)

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation
options.rationale: The pCO2 of 22 mmHg is appropriate compensation for an HCO3 of 8 mmol/L per Winter formula (expected 20 plus or minus 2 mmHg). This is compensatory Kussmaul breathing, not a primary respiratory alkalosis. A primary respiratory alkalosis would be suggested by pCO2 significantly lower than predicted. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from renal impairment
options.rationale: A concurrent non-anion gap metabolic acidosis would be suggested by a delta-delta ratio below 1 (delta AG less than delta HCO3). Here the delta-delta is 1.25, which is between 1 and 2, consistent with a pure HAGMA. While renal impairment is present, it is contributing to the HAGMA (uraemic acidosis) rather than causing a separate NAGMA. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis suggested by the delta-delta ratio
options.rationale: The anion gap is 32 (elevated by 20 above normal of 12). The HCO3 is 8 (decreased by 16 below normal of 24). The delta-delta ratio is 20/16 = 1.25. Strictly, a ratio between 1 and 2 is consistent with a pure HAGMA. However, in this clinical context with 3 days of vomiting (which causes metabolic alkalosis from HCl loss), the HCO3 should be even lower if the HAGMA were the only process. The delta AG exceeding the delta HCO3 (ratio above 1) in a vomiting patient suggests a concurrent metabolic alkalosis is partially offsetting the acidosis, raising the HCO3 above what pure DKA alone would produce. (Source: eTG: Respiratory; BMJ Best Practice: ABG Interpretation)

options.text: Mixed respiratory acidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis from COPD and diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: A respiratory acidosis would be indicated by an elevated pCO2. The pCO2 of 22 mmHg is low, reflecting appropriate respiratory compensation for the metabolic acidosis, not respiratory acidosis. Despite having COPD, this patient is able to mount an appropriate ventilatory response. Respiratory acidosis would be concerning if pCO2 were higher than predicted. (Source: eTG: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Systematic ABG interpretation requires a stepwise approach: identify the primary disturbance from pH, assess compensation, calculate the anion gap, and apply the delta-delta ratio to identify mixed disorders. In this case, the primary disturbance is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from DKA with uraemic contribution. The delta-delta ratio of 1.25, combined with the clinical history of prolonged vomiting, suggests a concurrent metabolic alkalosis that is partially masking the severity of the acidosis. Without the vomiting-induced alkalosis, the HCO3 would be even lower.
key_points: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3); normal approximately 12 in Australia
Delta-delta ratio = change in AG / change in HCO3; values above 1 may indicate concurrent metabolic alkalosis
Winter formula predicts expected pCO2 for respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis
Clinical context (vomiting) is essential for interpreting the delta-delta ratio
DKA and uraemia both contribute unmeasured anions to a high anion gap
explanation.pearls: In DKA with prolonged vomiting, the delta-delta ratio consistently exceeds 1.0 because gastric HCl loss generates a metabolic alkalosis that partially buffers the HCO3 fall - this hidden alkalosis means the HCO3 underestimates the true severity of ketoacid production.

subtopic_detail: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with osmolal gap - toxic alcohol
stem: A 45-year-old man is found confused in a park and brought to the emergency department by ambulance. He smells of alcohol. He is unable to provide a history. On examination he has nystagmus, ataxia, and appears intoxicated but there is no focal neurological deficit. His serum ethanol level returns as undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.4 C
data_table.Investigations: ABG: pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 6 mmol/L. Na 140 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cl 102 mmol/L, BSL 5.4 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, Cr 188 micromol/L, measured serum osmolality 326 mOsm/kg, calculated osmolality 289 mOsm/kg, urine microscopy: envelope-shaped crystals

lead_in: What is the most likely cause and the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Methanol poisoning - commence IV ethanol infusion and arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Methanol poisoning causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with osmolal gap but does NOT produce calcium oxalate crystals in urine. Methanol is metabolised to formic acid, which causes optic nerve toxicity. The envelope-shaped crystals (calcium oxalate monohydrate/dihydrate) are pathognomonic for ethylene glycol, not methanol. (Source: eTG: Toxicology; ANZCA Toxicology Guidelines)

options.text: Isopropanol ingestion - provide supportive care as this does not cause significant acidosis
options.rationale: Isopropanol is metabolised to acetone, which causes an osmolal gap and ketonaemia but NOT a significant anion gap metabolic acidosis. This patient has a severe HAGMA with pH 7.12 and HCO3 6 mmol/L, which excludes isopropanol as the sole ingestion. (Source: eTG: Toxicology)

options.text: Starvation ketoacidosis - administer IV dextrose and thiamine and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Starvation ketoacidosis produces elevated ketones and a HAGMA but would not cause an osmolal gap of 37 mOsm/kg or calcium oxalate crystalluria. The ketones here are only 0.4 mmol/L, which is normal. The osmolal gap and crystal pattern are diagnostic of toxic alcohol. (Source: eTG: Toxicology)

options.text: Ethylene glycol poisoning - administer IV fomepizole and arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: This is almost the correct answer, and IV fomepizole and haemodialysis are indeed the mainstay of treatment. However, the option text describes administering fomepizole alone before dialysis, whereas this patient meets criteria for immediate dialysis (pH below 7.15, renal failure, severe metabolic acidosis). Both must be commenced simultaneously. (Source: eTG: Toxicology)

options.text: Ethylene glycol poisoning - commence IV fomepizole and simultaneous urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: The combination of severe HAGMA (anion gap 32), large osmolal gap (326 - 289 = 37 mOsm/kg), undetectable ethanol, calcium oxalate crystalluria, and AKI is diagnostic of ethylene glycol poisoning. Fomepizole (15 mg/kg IV loading) inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, blocking conversion to glycolic and oxalic acids. Haemodialysis removes both the parent compound and toxic metabolites. Indications for dialysis include pH below 7.3, renal failure, or ethylene glycol level above 50 mg/dL. This patient meets multiple criteria. (Source: eTG: Toxicology; Toxicology Handbook)

explanation.summary: Ethylene glycol poisoning presents with an apparent intoxication (CNS depression, ataxia, nystagmus) that progresses through three stages: neurological, cardiopulmonary, and renal. The diagnostic hallmarks are severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, AKI, and calcium oxalate crystalluria on urine microscopy. Envelope-shaped crystals indicate calcium oxalate dihydrate. Treatment involves fomepizole to block alcohol dehydrogenase and urgent haemodialysis when pH is below 7.3, renal failure is present, or measured levels exceed 50 mg/dL.
key_points: Ethylene glycol causes HAGMA plus osmolal gap plus calcium oxalate crystalluria
Methanol causes HAGMA plus osmolal gap but no oxalate crystals and causes optic toxicity
Isopropanol causes osmolal gap and ketonaemia without significant HAGMA
Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose blocks alcohol dehydrogenase
Haemodialysis indications include pH below 7.3, renal failure, or level above 50 mg/dL
explanation.pearls: The osmolal gap may normalise despite worsening acidosis in late ethylene glycol poisoning because the parent compound has been fully metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acid - a normal osmolal gap does NOT exclude toxic alcohol ingestion if the presentation is delayed.

subtopic_detail: Lung cancer screening eligibility and LDCT referral
stem: A 58-year-old man presents for a routine health assessment. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and quit smoking 8 years ago. He has no respiratory symptoms. He asks about lung cancer screening after seeing a media report about the Australian lung cancer screening program.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Normal respiratory examination, no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding lung cancer screening eligibility?

options.text: He is eligible for biennial LDCT screening under the National Lung Cancer Screening Program
options.rationale: The Australian National Lung Cancer Screening Program (commenced 2025) offers biennial low-dose CT to adults aged 50 to 70 years with a 30 or more pack-year smoking history who are current smokers or have quit within the past 15 years. This patient meets all criteria: aged 58, 40-pack-year history, quit 8 years ago. LDCT screening reduces lung cancer mortality by approximately 20% based on the NELSON and NLST trials. (Source: Australian Government NLCSP; Cancer Council Australia)

options.text: He is ineligible because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago and his risk has normalised
options.rationale: Lung cancer risk remains substantially elevated for at least 15 years after smoking cessation. The Australian NLCSP eligibility extends to former smokers who quit within the past 15 years. Having quit 8 years ago, this patient remains within the eligible window. (Source: Australian Government NLCSP)

options.text: He should have an annual chest X-ray as the recommended initial lung cancer screening modality
options.rationale: Chest X-ray is not an effective lung cancer screening tool. Multiple randomised trials have shown no mortality reduction from chest X-ray screening. LDCT is the only imaging modality with proven mortality benefit for lung cancer screening. (Source: Cancer Council Australia; NLST)

options.text: He should undergo sputum cytology combined with spirometry as the recommended screening pathway
options.rationale: Sputum cytology has poor sensitivity for early-stage peripheral lung cancers and is not recommended for screening. Spirometry assesses airway function but does not detect lung cancer. Neither is part of the evidence-based screening pathway. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

options.text: He is ineligible because screening is only offered to current smokers with active respiratory symptoms
options.rationale: The NLCSP does not require current smoking status or respiratory symptoms. Screening targets asymptomatic high-risk individuals to detect early-stage disease before symptoms develop. Both current and recent former smokers meeting age and pack-year criteria are eligible. (Source: Australian Government NLCSP)

explanation.summary: Australia launched the National Lung Cancer Screening Program in 2025, offering biennial LDCT to high-risk individuals aged 50 to 70 with a 30 or more pack-year smoking history who are current smokers or quit within 15 years. This follows evidence from the NLST and NELSON trials showing 20 to 24% lung cancer mortality reduction with LDCT screening. The program includes shared decision-making, smoking cessation support, and structured reporting with standardised nodule management pathways.
key_points: LDCT is the only evidence-based lung cancer screening modality
Australian NLCSP eligibility: age 50 to 70, 30+ pack-years, current or quit within 15 years
Screening is biennial under the Australian program
LDCT screening reduces lung cancer mortality by approximately 20 to 24%
Chest X-ray and sputum cytology are not effective for lung cancer screening
explanation.pearls: The NELSON trial showed LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by 24% in men and up to 33% in women over 10 years - the Australian program adopted biennial rather than annual screening based on modelling showing comparable outcomes with lower cumulative radiation exposure and false positive rates.

subtopic_detail: Incidental lung mass urgent referral and staging workup
stem: A 64-year-old woman who is a current smoker (45 pack-years) presents with a 6-week history of persistent cough, haemoptysis, and unintentional weight loss of 4 kg. A chest X-ray shows a 3.5 cm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. She has no prior imaging for comparison.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CXR: 3.5 cm spiculated RUL mass with right hilar lymphadenopathy, FBC and UEC normal, calcium 2.82 mmol/L (corrected), LDH 310 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in the investigation pathway?

options.text: Refer for CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the lung mass before any further imaging
